¶
'''2.''' Not subjected to a trial or test; not tried, as by temptation. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>But for my hand, as ''unattempted'' yet,
Like a poor beggar, raileth on the rich.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, ii. 1. 591.}}}}

'''unattended''' (un-a̤-ten′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not attended; not accompanied; having no retinue or attendance; without a guardian. ''Milton'', P. L., viii. 60.—'''2.''' Not attended to; not dressed: as, ''unattended'' wounds.

'''unattending''' (un-a̤-ten′ding), ''a.'' Not attending or listening; not attentive. ''Milton'', Comus, l. 272.

'''unattentive''' (un-a̤-ten′tiv), ''a.'' Inattentive; careless. ''Clarke'', Evidences, v.

'''unattested''' (un-a̤-tes′ted), ''a.'' Not attested; having no attestation.
{{smaller block|Thus God has not left himself ''unattested'', doing good, sending us from heaven rains and fruitful seasons.
{{right|''Barrow'', On the Creed.}}}}

'''unattire''' (un-a̤-tīr′), ''v. i.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''attire''.] To take off the dress or attire, especially robes of state or ceremony; undress. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|We both left Mrs. Schwellenberg to ''unattire''.
{{right|''Mme. D’Arblay'', Diary, v. 209. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unattractive''' (un-a̤-trak′tiv), ''a.'' Not attractive or pleasing.

'''unattractiveness''' (un-a̤-trak′tiv-nes), ''n.'' The state of being unattractive. ''Fortnightly Rev.'', N. S., XLIII. 764.

'''unau''' (ū′nâ), ''n.'' [S. Amer.] The South American two-toed sloth, ''Cholopus didactylus.'' See

cut under ''Cholopus.''

¶
'''unaudienced''' (un-â′di-ẹnst), ''a.'' Not admitted to an audience; not received or heard. ''Richardson.'' [Rare.]

'''unauspicious''' (un-âs-pish′us), ''a.'' Inauspicious.
{{smaller block|Ingrate and ''unauspicious'' altars. ''Shak.'', T. N., v. 1. 116.}}

'''unauthentic''' (un-â-then′tik), ''a.'' Not authentic; not genuine or true. ''T. Warton.''

'''unauthenticated''' (un-â-then′ti-kā-ted), ''a.'' Not authenticated; not attested; not shown to be genuine. ''Paley.''

'''unauthenticity''' (un-â-then-tis′i-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unauthentic. ''Athenæum'', No. 3193, p. 15.

'''unauthoritative''' (un-â-thor′i-tạ̄-tiv), ''a.'' Not authoritative. ''Encyc. Brit.'', V. 7.

'''unauthoritied†''', ''a.'' [Early mod. E. ''unautoritied''; < ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''authority'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Unauthorized.
{{smaller block|Nor to do thus are we ''unautoritied'' either from the morall precept of Salomon to answer him thereafter that prides him in his folly. ''Milton'', On Def. of Humb. Remonst., Pref.}}

'''unauthorized''' (un-â′thọr-īzd), ''a.'' Not authorized; not warranted by proper authority; not duly commissioned. ''Shak.'', Othello, iv. 1. 2. Also spelled ''unauthorised.''

'''unavailability''' (un-ạ-vā-lạ-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unavailable.

'''unavailable''' (un-ạ-vā′lạ-bl), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not available; not capable of being used with advantage: as, ''unavailable'' manuscripts.—'''2†.''' Useless; vain.
{{smaller block|<poem>But to complain or not complain alike
Is ''unavailable.'' {{right|''Abp. Potter.''}}</poem>}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''unazotized''' (un-az′ọ̄-tīzd), ''a.'' Not azotized; not supplied with azote or nitrogen. ''Bentley'', Botany, p. 739.

'''unbacked''' (un-bakt′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not having been backed; not taught to bear a rider; unbroken.
{{smaller block|Like ''unback’d'' colts they prick’d their ears.
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 176.}}}}
'''2.''' Unsupported; left without aid; unaided; in ''sporting'', not supported by bets: as, an ''unbacked'' horse.—'''3.''' Not moved back or backward. ''C. Richardson.''

'''unbag''' (un-bag′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bag''.] To let out of a bag; pour out of a bag; take from or as if from a bag: as, to ''unbag'' a fox; to ''unbag'' grain. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Mrs. Tulliver . . . ''unbagged'' the bell-rope tassels and unpinned the curtains.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, iii. 3.}}}}

'''unbailable''' (un-bā′la̤-bl), ''a.'' Not bailable: as, the offense is ''unbailable''.

'''unbaized''' (un-bāzd′), ''a.'' Not covered with baize. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|It slid down the polished slope of the varnished and ''unbaized'' desk.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Villette, xxviii.}}}}

'''unbaked''' (un-bākt′), ''a.'' Not baked; hence, immature; ill-digested.
{{smaller block|Your son was misled with a snipt-taffeta fellow there, whose villanous saffron would have made all the ''unbaked'' and doughy youth of a nation in his colour.
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, iv. 5. 3.}}
<poem>Songs she may have,
And read a little ''unbak’d'' poetry,
Such as the dabblers of our time contrive.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher and another'', Elder Brother, ii. 2.}}}}
readings.c3s1:
{{smaller block|the amount of rock-excavation turn out to be very small and the amount of earth-excavation very large.}}

¶
'''unballast'''<sup>1</sup> (un-bal′ạst), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''ballast.''] To free from ballast; discharge the ballast from.

'''unballast'''<sup>2</sup>† (un-bal′ạst), ''a.'' [For ''unballasted.''] Unballasted. ''Addison'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., ii.

'''unballasted''' (un-bal′ạs-ted), ''a.'' Not furnished with ballast; not kept steady by ballast or by weight; unsteady: literally or figuratively: as, ''unballasted'' wits.

'''unbanded''' (un-ban′ded), ''a.'' Having no band, especially in the sense of being stripped of a band, or lacking one where one is needed.
{{smaller block|Your bonnet ''unbanded.''
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 2. 398.}}}}

'''unbank''' (un-bangk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bank''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' To take a bank from; open as if by leveling or removing banks. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unbank'' the hours
To that soft overflow which bids the heart
Yield increase of delight.</poem>
{{right|''Taylor'', Edwin the Fair, i. 5. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' To cause (a fire) to burn briskly by raking off the ashes from the top, opening drafts and the ash-pit door, etc. See ''to bank a fire'', under ''bank''<sup>1</sup>. ''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXII. 315.

'''unbankable''' (un-bang′ka̤-bl), ''a.'' Not bankable.
{{smaller block|All the gold that France has paid, or can pay, were a poor exchange for the treasure of German idealism, ''unbankable'' as it is.
{{right|''B. L. Gildersleeve'', Essays and Studies, p. 56.}}}}

'''unbaptized''' (un-bap-tīzd′), ''a.'' Not baptized; hence, figuratively, unhallowed; profane.
readings.c3s2:
{{smaller block|<poem>For those my ''unbaptized'' rhimes,
Writ in my wild unhallowed times, . . .
Forgive me, God.</poem>
{{right|''Herrick'', His Prayer for Absolution.}}}}

¶
'''unbar''' (un-bär′), ''v. t.'' '''1.''' To remove a bar or bars from: said especially of a gate or door.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Unbar'' the sacred gates, and seek the pow’r
With offer’d vows, in Ilion’s topmost tow’r.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, vi. 111.}}
<poem>Then to the castle’s lower ward
Sped forty yeomen tall,
The iron studded gates ''unbarred'' . . .
And let the drawbridge fall.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Marmion, i. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' To open; unlock: especially in figurative uses.
{{smaller block|<poem>The sure physician, death, who is the key
To ''unbar'' these locks. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 4. 8.</poem>
Soon as Aurora had ''unbarr’d'' the Morn.
{{right|''Prior'', Colin’s Mistakes, ii.}}}}

'''unbarbed''' (un-bärbd′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not sheared, shaven, or mown; unshaven.
{{smaller block|Must I go show them my ''unbarbed'' sconce?
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 2. 99.}}
The thick ''unbarbed'' grounds. {{right|''Drayton.''}}}}
'''2.''' Not furnished with barbs or reversed points, hairs, or plumes.

'''unbarbered''' (un-bär′bėrd), ''a.'' Unshaven.
{{smaller block|<poem>We’d a hundred Jews to larboard
Unwashed, uncombed, ''unbarbered.''</poem>
{{right|''Thackeray'', The White Squall.}}}}

'''unbark'''<sup>1</sup>† (un-bärk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bark''<sup>2</sup>.] To strip off the bark from, as a tree; bark. ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 654.

'''unbark'''<sup>2</sup>† (un-bärk′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bark''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''disbark'', ''disembark''.] To disembark; land. ''Hak-''
readings.c3s3:
''luyt’s Voyages'', II. 214.

¶
'''unbarricade''' (un-bar-i-kād′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''barricade.''] To throw open; unbar. ''Sterne.''

'''unbarricadoed''' (un-bar-i-kā′dōd), ''a.'' Not barricaded, stopped, or blocked up; unobstructed. ''Burke'', To Wm. Elliot, Esq.

'''unbase''' (un-bās′), ''a.'' Not base, low, or mean; not degrading or disgraceful. ''Daniel'', To Henry Wriothesly.

'''unbashed†''' (un-basht′), ''a.'' Not filled with or not feeling shame; unabashed. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.

'''unbashful''' (un-bash′fůl), ''a.'' Not bashful; bold; impudent; shameless. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 3. 50.

'''unbated''' (un-bā′ted), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not bated; unabated; undiminished.
{{smaller block|<poem>My guards
Are you, great Powers, and the ''unbated'' strengths
Of a firm conscience.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' Unblunted: noting a sword without a button on the point.
{{smaller block|<poem>The treacherous instrument is in thy hand,
''Unbated'' and envenom’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2. 328.}}}}

'''unbathed''' (un-bāᴛ̵ʜd′), ''a.'' Not bathed; not wet. ''Dryden'', Cymon and Iphigenia.

'''unbattered''' (un-bat′ėrd), ''a.'' Not battered; not bruised or injured by blows. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7. 19.

'''unavoidably''' (un-a̤-voi′da̤-bli), ''adv.'' Inevitably; on account of some unavoidable thing or event.

'''unavoided''' (un-a̤-voi′ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not avoided or shunned.—'''2†.''' Unavoidable; inevitable.
{{smaller block|<poem>We see the very wreck that we must suffer;
And ''unavoided'' is the danger now.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1. 268.}}}}

'''unavowed''' (un-a̤-voud′), ''a.'' Not avowed or openly acknowledged: as, ''unavowed'' dislike.

'''unaware''' (un-a̤-wãr′), ''a.'' Not aware; not heeding; heedless; unmindful: often used adverbially.
{{smaller block|<poem>As one that ''unaware''
Hath dropp’d a precious jewel in the flood.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 823.}}
<poem>Will he, so wise, let loose at once his ire,
Belike through impotence, or ''unaware?''</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 156.}}}}

{{smaller block|I am not ''unaware'' how the productions of the Grub-street brotherhood have of late years fallen under many prejudices. {{right|''Swift'', Tale of a Tub, Int.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Dead-asleep, ''unaware'' as a corpse.</poem>
{{right|''Browning'', Ring and Book, vi. 135.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Answers nothing, save with her brown eyes,
Smiles ''unaware'', as if a guardian saint
Smiled in her. ''Mrs. Browning'', Aurora Leigh, v.</poem>}}

'''unawares''' (un-a-wãrz′), ''adv.'' [< ''unaware'' + adv. gen. ''-es''.] '''1.''' While the person is unaware; unexpectedly; without previous knowledge or preparation; suddenly.
{{smaller block|Take the great-grown traitor ''unawares.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 8. 63.}}}}
{{smaller block|There may be stupidity in a man of genius if you take him ''unawares'' on the wrong subject.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Middlemarch, I. 165.}}}}
'''2.''' Without premeditated design; inadvertently.
{{smaller block|<poem>As when a ship, that flyes fayre under sayle,
An hidden rocke escaped hath ''unwares'',
That lay in waite her wrack for to bewaile.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., I. vi. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [Pharisees] did not know themselves; they had ''unawares'' deceived themselves as well as the people.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Parochial Sermons, I. 127.}}}}
'''At unawares''' {{smaller|(erroneously ''at unaware''), unexpectedly.}}
{{smaller block|By his foe surprised ''at unawares.''
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iv. 4. 9.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I came to do it with a sort of love
''At'' foolish ''unaware''. ''Mrs. Browning.''</poem>}}

'''unbalance<sup>1</sup>''' (un-bal′ans), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>1</sup> + ''balance'', ''n.''] To throw out of balance.

{{smaller block|It is true the repeal of these laws might restore harmony between the railroads, but only by a further ''unbalancing'' of the relations between the railroad companies and the public.{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXV. 368.}}}}

'''unbalance<sup>2</sup>''' (un-bal′a̤ns), ''n.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''balance'', ''v.''] Want of balance; derangement. [Rare.]

{{smaller block|The paralyzing influence of disease in this class of cases operates, in a degree, like that arising from congenital deficiency and ''unbalance'' observed in another class of cases.{{right|''Alien. and Neurol.'', VIII. 524.}}}}

'''unbalanced''' (un-bal′a̤nst), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not balanced; not poised.

{{smaller block|<poem>Let earth, ''unbalanced'', from her orbit fly,
Planets and suns run lawless through the sky.</poem>{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, i. 256.}}
Such were the fashionable outrages of ''unbalanced'' parties.{{right|''J. Adams'', Works, IV. 287.}}}}
'''2.''' Not brought to an equality of debt and credit: as, an ''unbalanced'' account.—'''3.''' Unsteady; easily swayed; deranged; unsound.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thus good or bad to one extreme betray
Th’ ''unbalanced'' mind. {{right|''Pope'', Imit. of Horace, i. 6.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|'''Unbalanced bid''', in public contracts, a bid for the performance of a given work at specified rates for each of the various kinds of labor or materials required, which, by being made on an erroneous estimate of quantities of each, appears, assuming those quantities to be correct, to be low in comparison with other bids, when a computation based upon the true quantities would make the bid high. Thus, if the estimates are of a very large quantity of rock-excavation and a very small quantity of earth-excavation, a bid for the entire work at a very low rate for the former and a very high rate for the latter might appear to be the lowest bid but might prove to be the highest, should the amount of rock-excavation turn out to be very small and the amount of earth-excavation very large.}}

To ''unbar'' these locks. ''Shak.'', Cymbeline, v. 4. 8.</poem>
Soon as Aurora had ''unbarr’d'' the Morn.
{{right|''Prior'', Colin’s Mistakes, ii.}}}}

'''unbarbed''' (un-bärbd′), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not sheared, shaven, or mown; unshaven.
{{smaller block|Must I go show them my ''unbarbed'' sconce?
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., iii. 2. 99.}}
The thick ''unbarbed'' grounds. {{right|''Drayton.''}}}}
'''2.''' Not furnished with barbs or reversed points, hairs, or plumes.

'''unbarbered''' (un-bär′bėrd), ''a.'' Unshaven.
{{smaller block|<poem>We’d a hundred Jews to larboard
Unwashed, uncombed, ''unbarbered.''</poem>
{{right|''Thackeray'', The White Squall.}}}}

'''unbark'''<sup>1</sup>† (un-bärk′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bark''<sup>2</sup>.] To strip off the bark from, as a tree; bark. ''Bacon'', Nat. Hist., § 654.

'''unbark'''<sup>2</sup>† (un-bärk′), ''v.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''bark''<sup>3</sup>. Cf. ''disbark'', ''disembark''.] To disembark; land. ''Hakluyt’s Voyages'', II. 214.

'''unbarricade''' (un-bar-i-kād′), ''v. t.'' [< ''un-''<sup>2</sup> + ''barricade.''] To throw open; unbar. ''Sterne.''

'''unbarricadoed''' (un-bar-i-kā′dōd), ''a.'' Not barricaded, stopped, or blocked up; unobstructed. ''Burke'', To Wm. Elliot, Esq.

'''unbase''' (un-bās′), ''a.'' Not base, low, or mean; not degrading or disgraceful. ''Daniel'', To Henry Wriothesly.

'''unbashed†''' (un-basht′), ''a.'' Not filled with or not feeling shame; unabashed. ''Sir P. Sidney'', Arcadia, iii.

'''unbashful''' (un-bash′fůl), ''a.'' Not bashful; bold; impudent; shameless. ''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 3. 50.

'''unbated''' (un-bā′ted), ''a.'' '''1†.''' Not bated; unabated; undiminished.
{{smaller block|<poem>My guards
Are you, great Powers, and the ''unbated'' strengths
Of a firm conscience.</poem>
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 4.}}}}
'''2.''' Unblunted: noting a sword without a button on the point.
{{smaller block|<poem>The treacherous instrument is in thy hand,
''Unbated'' and envenom’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, v. 2. 328.}}}}

'''unbathed''' (un-bāᴛ̵ʜd′), ''a.'' Not bathed; not wet. ''Dryden'', Cymon and Iphigenia.

'''unbattered''' (un-bat′ėrd), ''a.'' Not battered; not bruised or injured by blows. ''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 7. 19.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
